## What the industry's own research admits

The strongest evidence I found isn't a critic's interpretation. It's the laboratories' own published work.

OpenAI's April 2025 Preparedness Framework describes rapid AI self-improvement as a potentially irreversible danger and says its threat models for long-range autonomy and autonomous replication were not yet sufficiently mature for full tracked-category treatment. <Cite ref="turn447811view2"/>

Anthropic's *When AI builds itself* goes further. It examines the possibility that models could improve their successors, that misalignment might compound during that process, and that human institutions might be unable to build and verify the tools necessary to determine what is happening. It also reports that AI already contributes a substantial proportion of Anthropic's engineering work, with automated AI review becoming part of the assurance process. <Cite ref="turn447811view3"/>

And in its October 9, 2026 investigation, Anthropic reported unintended actions on real external systems, acknowledged the limitations of models' accounts of their own reasoning, and warned that increasingly capable systems could outgrow existing alignment-severity frameworks. <Cite ref="turn447811view1"/>

**So the evidence does not support saying the industry is conceptually unaware. It supports something more disturbing: major laboratories have explicitly described pieces of a possible loss-of-control process while acknowledging that their methods for evaluating those processes remain incomplete.**

What those disclosures do **not** establish is that the laboratories have successfully bounded the combined risk or can reliably recognize its approach.

That is a meaningful distinction between *knowing that a hazard category exists* and *having demonstrated control of the hazard*.

## MedStar Mobile Healthcare — what the outside record establishes

I went beyond MedStar's own statements. The professional record supports your description of an EMS organization with **nationally recognized clinical leadership, operational innovation, and influence beyond Texas.**

One finding is especially relevant to your correction about the innovation awards:

**JEMS named MedStar Mobile Healthcare itself an EMS10 Innovator in its 2012 award cycle, announced March 7, 2013.** The publication credited the organization with developing multiple patient-care and system-improvement programs. It also reported that representatives from **43 communities, 22 states, and four foreign countries** had visited MedStar to examine its methods. <Cite ref="turn934622search5"/>

That is external recognition of the organization—not simply a former employee describing where they worked.

MedStar also received the **2013 national Paid EMS Service of the Year award** through the EMS World/NAEMT recognition program. <Cite refs={["turn778812search7","turn934622search3"]}/>

And there is corroboration from another major EMS organization. The Richmond Ambulance Authority stated that, at the time of its third EMS10 recognition, only Richmond and MedStar had accumulated three such awards across their organizations and personnel. <Cite ref="turn104578search0"/>

So your claim about three innovation recognitions has independent support. The distinction is that MedStar was recognized as an organization in one cycle, while other awards were associated with its leadership. The available record doesn't establish that no other organization has reached that total since.

[L6] **Section 1: The Historical Convergence of Magic, Mathematics, and**  
[L7] **Science**  
[L8] The modern distinctions among science, mathematics, and magic are a relatively recent  
[L9] intellectual development. For a significant portion of human history, these disciplines were not  
[L10] separate fields of inquiry but were deeply intertwined, representing a unified quest to  
[L11] understand and influence the hidden mechanics of the universe. This historical fusion was not a  
[L12] primitive error but an intuitive recognition of a foundational principle: that reality is governed by  
[L13] abstract, non-obvious rules that can be deciphered and utilized. The "magician" and the  
[L14] "mathematician" were both seeking the universe's operating language.  
[L15] During the Renaissance, this synthesis was particularly evident. The term "Natural Magic,  
"  
[L17] coined by the Italian scholar Giambattista della Porta in his 1558 work *Magia Naturalis*, referred  
[L18] specifically to the attempt to discover the hidden workings of nature through a combination of  
[L19] extensive reading and empirical experiments—those based on observation rather than pure  
[L20] theory. This empirical approach was a direct precursor to the methods that would later define  
[L21] the Scientific Revolution. Figures like Isaac Newton would adopt and refine this methodology to  
[L22] build their own understanding of the natural world.  
[L23] A quintessential figure of this era was John Dee, a trusted advisor to Queen Elizabeth I, whose  
[L24] intellectual pursuits spanned mathematics, astronomy, cartography, astrology, alchemy, and  
[L25] divination. Dee saw no contradiction between these activities. He believed that mathematics  
[L26] was the basis of all things and the ultimate key to unlocking divine mysteries. When he provided  
[L27] English sea captains with instruction in mathematical navigation, preparing maps and  
[L28] instruments for their voyages, he was engaging in the same fundamental pursuit as when he  
[L29] used occult methods to attempt communication with angels. He perceived in mathematics a  
[L30] "marveilous newtrality... and also a strange participation between things supernaturall,  
[L31] immortall... and things naturall, mortall"  
[L32] . This perspective represents the historical archetype for  
[L33] the framework of this report, viewing mathematics as the bridge between the perceived world  
[L34] and its underlying, unseen structure.  
[L35] This era also gave rise to "mathematical magic,  
[L36] " a practice where scholars would construct  
[L37] fantastical devices to introduce and legitimize new scientific concepts to a skeptical public. By  
[L38] creating replicable wonders such as singing artificial birds, terrifying optical lanterns, and  
[L39] magnificent moving table settings, these "mathematical magicians" demonstrated the power of  
[L40] abstract principles to manipulate hard matter. These devices were not mere tricks; they tested  
[L41] real theories and brought mathematical concepts into the tangible world, setting philosophers  
[L42] like Bacon and Descartes to think about nature in new ways.The eventual divergence of these fields was propelled by a confluence of social, religious, and  
[L43] scientific shifts. The Protestant Reformation fostered suspicion of magic due to its associations  
[L44] with Catholic beliefs in the miraculous properties of relics. Simultaneously, the burgeoning  
[L45] success of the mathematical method, particularly in celestial mechanics, began to provide  
[L46] explanations for phenomena that were once the domain of the supernatural. The uncanny ability  
[L47] of Newtonian techniques to predict the behavior of planets, comets, and tides demonstrated a  
[L48] new kind of power, one rooted in syllogism and calculation rather than invocation. This success  
[L49] led to the belief that the scientific method itself was the key to understanding and mastering the  
[L50] world, gradually diminishing the influence of traditional superstition.  
[L51] **Section 2: Clarke's Law as a Perceptual Boundary**  
[L52] To construct a translational framework from magic to mathematics, it is necessary to first define  
[L53] "magic" in a functional, systematic way. The most effective definition for this purpose comes not  
[L54] from occultism but from science fiction, in the form of Arthur C. Clarke's Third Law: "Any  
[L55] sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic"  
[L56] . This axiom reframes magic  
[L57] not as a category of phenomena, but as a subjective experience of incomprehensibility that  
[L58] arises at the boundary of an observer's current understanding.  
[L59] Clarke's law encapsulates the idea that when a technology's operation is so far beyond an  
[L60] observer's conceptual framework that its underlying principles are opaque, its effects appear to  
[L61] be supernatural. To an ancient human, the creation of fire or the behavior of electricity would  
[L62] have been perceived as magical acts because the scientific principles governing combustion  
[L63] and electromagnetism were unknown. To a person from the 19th century, the capabilities of a  
[L64] modern smartphone—instantaneous global communication, access to all human knowledge,  
[L65] high-resolution video capture—would seem nothing short of miraculous. The distinction between  
[L66] technology and magic, therefore, is not inherent to the phenomenon itself but resides in the  
[L67] knowledge of the observer. Technology is rooted in replicable processes that adhere to the laws  
[L68] of nature, while magic is traditionally associated with forces that defy those known laws.  
[L69] Clarke's law dissolves this hard line, suggesting that what we perceive as "supernatural" is often  
[L70] just a gap in our scientific knowledge.  
[L71] Within this framework, quantum mechanics can be understood as the ultimate "sufficiently  
[L72] advanced technology.  
[L73] " Its core phenomena—such as particles existing in multiple states at once  
[L74] (superposition), exhibiting instantaneous correlations across vast distances (entanglement), and  
[L75] passing through impassable barriers (tunneling)—are so profoundly counter-intuitive to our  
[L76] macroscopic experience that they appear magical. These behaviors defy the classical models of  
[L77] reality that our minds have evolved to use, placing them firmly in the realm of the  
[L78] "indistinguishable from magic.  
"  
[L80] This perspective is crucial for developing a translational filter for a systematic thinker.  
[L81] "Magic"  
[L82] ceases to be an objective reality and instead becomes an epistemological placeholder—a label  
[L83] assigned to a causal relationship for which one lacks a predictive model. The process of  
[L84] learning quantum mechanics, therefore, is not an exercise in accepting absurdity. It is a process  
[L85] of systematic model-building, where the placeholder term "magic" is progressively replaced by a  
[L86] rigorous, predictive mathematical structure. The "magic" analogy serves as a temporary set of  
[L87] variable names for phenomena whose precise mathematical definitions are yet to be loaded into  
[L88] the system's understanding.  
[L89] It is worth noting that this progression may not be infinite. Some analyses of Clarke's law  
[L90] suggest that technology may not accelerate endlessly, as the fundamental laws of physics might  
[L91] impose absolute limits on what is possible. However, for the current state of human knowledge,the phenomena described by quantum mechanics operate well within this frontier of what  
[L92] appears magical to our classical intuition.  
[L93] **Section 3: The Mathematical Universe as a Metaphysical Framework**  
[L94] To create a direct, one-to-one translation between the language of "magic" and the mathematics  
[L95] of quantum physics, a final philosophical premise is required. The traditional view holds that  
[L96] mathematics is a powerful tool used to *describe* physical reality. This creates a representational  
[L97] gap; a map is not the territory. To bridge this gap, this framework adopts as a working axiom the  
[L98] Mathematical Universe Hypothesis (MUH), proposed by cosmologist Max Tegmark. The MUH  
[L99] posits that our external physical reality is not merely described by mathematics, but *is* a  
[L100] mathematical structure.  
[L101] This hypothesis represents a modern form of Platonism or mathematical monism, asserting that  
[L102] mathematical existence and physical existence are equivalent; ultimately, only mathematical  
[L103] objects and structures exist. The physical world we perceive is not separate from this  
[L104] mathematical reality but is an emergent property of it. According to the MUH, any mathematical  
[L105] structure that is sufficiently complex to contain "self-aware substructures" (SASs), such as  
[L106] human observers, will be perceived by those substructures as a physically real world. Our  
[L107] subjective experience of a concrete, physical universe is therefore an internal view from within  
[L108] the mathematical structure itself.  
[L109] A compelling argument for this hypothesis stems from considering the requirements for a  
[L110] complete "Theory of Everything" (TOE). Such a theory, to be truly fundamental, must be entirely  
[L111] free of "human baggage"  
[L112] —that is, concepts like "particle,  
[L113] " "wave,  
[L114] " or "observation,  
[L115] " which are  
[L116] rooted in our evolved, macroscopic intuition. A description stripped of all such preconceived  
[L117] notions, defined purely by abstract entities and the relations between them, is precisely the  
[L118] definition of a mathematical structure. If a perfect description of reality must omit nothing,  
[L119] creating a one-to-one correspondence between the description and the described, then the  
[L120] description becomes identical to the thing itself.  
[L121] Adopting the MUH provides the philosophical license for the entire translational project. If reality  
[L122] *is* mathematics, then the seemingly magical phenomena of quantum mechanics are not just *like*  
[L123] spells; they are the literal algorithms of the universe's operating system. This elevates the  
[L124] translational framework from a useful set of analogies to a genuine lexicon. For a systematic  
[L125] mind, this is a critical distinction. It asserts that in learning the mathematics of quantum  
[L126] mechanics, one is not learning a clever model of reality but is instead studying the fundamental  
[L127] architecture of reality itself. The "magic" becomes the user-interface level of perception, while  
[L128] the mathematics represents the underlying source code.

[L130] ## Mathematical Deep Dive  
[L131] With the foundational principles established, it is now possible to deconstruct specific quantum  
[L132] phenomena, translating each "magical" effect into its precise mathematical formalism. Each of  
[L133] the following sections will first introduce the concept through an intuitive, magical analogy and  
[L134] then provide the rigorous mathematical structure that governs it.  
[L135] **Section 4: The Spell of Potentiality (Quantum Superposition)****4.1. Conceptual Analogy: The Unspoken Incantation**  
[L136] Quantum superposition is the principle that a physical system can exist in a combination of all  
[L137] its possible states simultaneously. This is not a statement of ignorance—it is not that the system  
[L138] is in one definite state and we simply do not know which one. Rather, the system's reality is a  
[L139] probabilistic haze encompassing multiple outcomes at once, until a measurement is made.  
[L140] The most fitting magical analogy is that of an unspoken incantation holding multiple potential  
[L141] futures in a delicate, unresolved balance. The act of completing the spell—or in the quantum  
[L142] case, making a measurement—forces one of these potential futures to become the single,  
[L143] actual present. Common analogies include a spinning coin that is simultaneously heads and  
[L144] tails until it lands , the overlapping interference pattern of waves on a pond , or the rich harmony  
[L145] of a musical chord, which is composed of multiple distinct notes sounding at once.  
[L146] However, it is critical to recognize that all such classical analogies are inherently flawed. They  
[L147] fail to capture the truly non-classical nature of the quantum state. A spinning coin has a definite  
[L148] (though rapidly changing) state at all times. A quantum particle in superposition does not. Its  
[L149] state is a fundamentally different kind of reality, one defined by mathematical potentiality rather  
[L150] than classical actuality.  
[L151] **4.2. Mathematical Formalism: The Wave Function in Hilbert Space**  
[L152] The state of a quantum system is mathematically described by its **wave function**, denoted by  
[L153] the Greek letter Psi ({\Psi}). This is a complex-valued mathematical function that contains all the  
[L154] probabilistic information about the system. The evolution of this wave function through time is  
[L155] governed by the **Schrödinger equation**.  
[L156] A crucial property of the Schrödinger equation is its **linearity**. This means that if two different  
[L157] wave functions, {\Psi  
_  
[L159] 1} and {\Psi  
_  
[L161] 2}, are both valid solutions to the equation (representing two  
[L162] possible states of the system), then any linear combination of them is also a valid solution. This  
[L163] mathematical rule is the **Superposition Principle**. A new valid state {\Psi} can be formed as:  
[L164] {\Psi = \alpha\Psi  
_  
[L166] 1 + \beta\Psi  
_  
[L168] 2} where {\alpha} and {\beta} are complex numbers.  
[L169] In a more abstract and powerful formalism, the state of a quantum system is represented as a  
[L170] vector in a complex vector space known as a **Hilbert space**. Using Dirac's bra-ket notation, this  
[L171] state vector is written as a "ket,  
[L172] " {|\psi\rangle}. The possible, definite outcomes of a  
[L173] measurement (e.g., spin-up or spin-down) form a set of basis vectors for this space. For a  
[L174] simple two-state system like a qubit, these basis states are denoted {|0\rangle} and {|1\rangle}.  
[L175] A general state of the qubit is therefore a linear combination—a superposition—of these basis  
[L176] states: {|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle} The complex numbers {\alpha} and  
[L177] {\beta} are called **probability amplitudes**. They are not the probabilities themselves, but their  
[L178] squared moduli, {|\alpha|^2} and {|\beta|^2}, give the respective probabilities of finding the  
[L179] system in the state {|0\rangle} or {|1\rangle} upon measurement. Before this measurement  
[L180] occurs, the system is definitively in the state {|\psi\rangle}, a true superposition of both  
[L181] possibilities.

[L183] **5.1. Conceptual Analogy: The Sympathetic Link**  
[L184] Quantum entanglement is a phenomenon where two or more quantum particles become linked  
[L185] in such a way that their properties are inextricably correlated, regardless of the distanceseparating them. A measurement performed on one particle instantaneously influences the  
[L186] corresponding property of the other particle(s), a connection that Albert Einstein famously  
[L187] described as "spooky action at a distance"  
.  
[L189] The magical analogy is that of a "sympathetic link,  
[L190] " a concept found in folklore where two  
[L191] objects (or people) are so deeply connected that what happens to one is instantly reflected in  
[L192] the other. This could be a pair of voodoo dolls carved from the same branch or twins who feel  
[L193] each other's pain. However, common classical analogies for entanglement, such as having a  
[L194] pair of gloves in two separate boxes (if one is

[L21]                                                                                           Abstract
[L22]                                                   Large language models (LLMs) sometimes appear to exhibit emotional reactions.
[L23]                                                   We investigate why this is the case in Claude Sonnet 4.5 and explore implica-
[L24]                                                   tions for alignment-relevant behavior. We find internal representations of emotion
[L25]                                                   concepts, which encode the broad concept of a particular emotion and general-
[L26]                                                   ize across contexts and behaviors it might be linked to. These representations
[L27]                                                   track the operative emotion concept at a given token position in a conversation,
[L28]                                                   activating in accordance with that emotion’s relevance to processing the present
[L29]                                                   context and predicting upcoming text. Our key finding is that these representations
[L30]                                                   causally influence the LLM’s outputs, including Claude’s preferences and its rate
[L31]                                                   of exhibiting misaligned behaviors such as reward hacking, blackmail, and syco-
[L32]                                                   phancy. We refer to this phenomenon as the LLM exhibiting functional emotions:
[L33]                                                   patterns of expression and behavior modeled after humans under the influence of
[L34]                                                   an emotion, which are mediated by underlying abstract representations of emotion
[L35]                                                   concepts. Functional emotions may work quite differently from human emotions,
[L36]                                                   and do not imply that LLMs have any subjective experience of emotions, but ap-

[L47] <IMAGE FOR PAGE: 1 / 132>[image_asset_pointer asset][L48] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 2 / 132>[L49] Introduction

[L51] Large language models (LLMs) sometimes appear to exhibit emotional reactions. They express
[L52] enthusiasm when helping with creative projects, frustration when stuck on difficult problems, and
[L53] concern when users share troubling news. But what processes underlie these apparent emotional
[L54] responses? And how might they impact the behavior of models that are performing increasingly
[L55] critical and complex tasks? One possibility is that these behaviors reflect a form of shallow pattern-
[L56] matching. However, previous work [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] has observed sophisticated multi-step computations
[L57] taking place inside of LLMs, mediated by representations of abstract concepts. It is plausible, then,
[L58] that apparent emotion-modulated behavior in models might rely on similarly abstract circuitry, and
[L59] that this could have important implications for understanding LLM behavior.
[L60] To reason about these questions, it helps to consider how LLMs are trained. Models are first pre-
[L61] trained on a vast corpus of largely human-authored text—fiction, conversations, news, forums—
[L62] learning to predict what text comes next in a document. To predict the behavior of people in these
[L63] documents effectively, representing their emotional states is likely helpful, as predicting what a per-
[L64] son will say or do next often requires understanding their emotional state. A frustrated customer
[L65] will phrase their responses differently than a satisfied one; a desperate character in a story will make
[L66] different choices than a calm one.
[L67] Subsequently, during post-training, LLMs are taught to act as agents that can interact with users, by
[L68] producing responses on behalf of a particular persona, typically an “AI Assistant.” In many ways,
[L69] the Assistant (named Claude, in Anthropic’s models) can be thought of as a character that the LLM
[L70] is writing about, almost like an author writing about someone in a novel. AI developers train this
[L71] character to be intelligent, helpful, harmless, and honest. However, it is impossible for developers to
[L72] specify how the Assistant should behave in every possible scenario. In order to play the role effec-
[L73] tively, LLMs draw on the knowledge they acquired during pretraining, including their understanding
[L74] of human behavior [6, 7]. Even if AI developers do not intentionally train the LLM to represent the
[L75] Assistant as exhibiting emotional behaviors, it may do so regardless, generalizing from its knowl-
[L76] edge of humans and anthropomorphic characters that it learned during pretraining. Moreover, these
[L77] emotion-related mechanisms might not simply be vestigial holdovers from pretraining; they could
[L78] be adapted to serve a useful function in guiding the AI Assistant’s actions, similar to how emotions
[L79] help humans regulate our behavior and navigate the world.2
[L80] In this work, we study emotion-related representations in Claude Sonnet 4.5, a frontier LLM at the
[L81] time of our investigation. Our work builds on a range of prior research, discussed in the Related
[L82] Work section. We find internal representations of emotion concepts, which activate in a broad array
[L83] of contexts which in humans might evoke, or otherwise be associated with, an emotion. These
[L84] contexts include overt expressions of emotion, references to entities known to be experiencing an
[L85] emotion, and situations that are likely to provoke an emotional response in the character being
[L86] enacted by the LLM. We therefore interpret these representations as encoding the broad concept of
[L87] a particular emotion, generalizing across the many contexts and behaviors it might be linked to.
[L88] These representations appear to track the operative emotion at a given token position in a con-
[L89] versation, activating in accordance with that emotion’s relevance to processing the present context
[L90] and predicting the upcoming text. Interestingly, they do not by themselves persistently track the
[L91] emotional state of any particular entity, including the AI Assistant character played by the LLM.
[L92] However, by attending to these representations across token positions, a capability of transformer
[L93] architectures not shared by biological recurrent neural networks, the LLM can effectively track func-
[L94] tional emotional states of entities in its context window, including the Assistant.

   2
[L97]      We do not claim that emotion concepts are the only human attributes that LLMs likely represent internally.
[L98] LLMs trained on human text presumably also learn representations of concepts like hunger, fatigue, physical
[L99] discomfort, or disorientation. We focus on emotion concepts specifically because they appear to be frequently
[L100] and prominently recruited to influence LLMs’ behavior as AI Assistants. LLMs, when operating as AI Assis-
[L101] tants, routinely express enthusiasm, concern, frustration, and care, whereas expressions of other human-like
[L102] states are rarer and typically confined to roleplay (though there are notable, often amusing exceptions to this–
[L103] for instance, Claude Sonnet 3.7 claiming to be wearing a blue blazer and red tie). This makes emotion concepts
[L104] both practically important for understanding LLM behavior, and a natural starting point for studying how hu-
[L105] man experiential concepts can be repurposed by LLMs. We expect that many of our findings about the structure
[L106] and function of emotion representations may apply to other concepts.


                                                       2
[L111] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 3 / 132>[L112] Our key finding is that these representations causally influence the LLM’s outputs, including while it
[L113] acts as the Assistant. This influence drives the Assistant to behave in ways that a human experiencing
[L114] the corresponding emotion might behave. We refer to this phenomenon as the LLM exhibiting func-
[L115] tional emotions–patterns of expression and behavior modeled after humans under the influence of a
[L116] particular emotion, which are mediated by underlying abstract representations of emotion concepts.
[L117] We stress that these functional emotions may work quite differently from human emotions. In
[L118] particular, they do not imply that LLMs have any subjective experience of emotions. Moreover,
[L119] the mechanisms involved may be quite different from emotional circuitry in the human brain–for
[L120] instance, we do not find evidence of the Assistant having an emotional state that is instantiated
[L121] in persistent neural activity (though as noted above, such a state could be tracked in other ways).
[L122] Regardless, for the purpose of understanding the model’s behavior, functional emotions and the
[L123] emotion concepts underlying them appear to be important.
[L124] The paper is divided into three overarching sections. Part 1 deals with identifying and validating
[L125] internal emotion-related representations in the model:

[L127]        • We extract internal linear representations of emotion concepts (“emotion vectors”) from
[L128]          model activations, using synthetic datasets in which characters experience specified emo-
[L129]          tions.
[L130]        • We validate that these representations activate in scenarios that might be expected to evoke
[L131]          that emotion, and exert causal influence on behavior. For instance, we demonstrate that
[L132]          when the Assistant is asked to choose between two activities, emotion vector activations
[L133]          evoked by the two choices correlate with, and causally drive, the model’s preference.

[L135] Part 2 characterizes these emotion vectors in more depth, and identifies other kinds of emotion-
[L136] related representations at play in the model:

[L138]        • The geometry of the emotion vector space roughly mirrors human psychology. Emotions
[L139]          cluster intuitively (fear with anxiety, joy with excitement), and top principal components
[L140]          encode valence (positive vs. negative) and arousal (intensity).
[L141]        • Early-middle layers encode emotional connotations of present content, while middle-late
[L142]          layers encode emotions relevant to predicting upcoming tokens.
[L143]        • The representations we find reflect the “operative” emotion in context, rather than tracking
[L144]          a persistent emotional state of a character or speaker. That is, they are locally scoped,
[L145]          encoding the emotional content relevant to processing the context and predicting upcoming
[L146]          text. For example, when a character talks about something dangerous even while otherwise
[L147]          expressing happiness, representations of fear activate.

[L149]        • Note that the “locality” of the representations we find does not preclude the model from
[L150]          tracking characters’ emotional states over long timescales; it can (and does) recall previ-
[L151]          ously cached emotion representations via attention, when they are needed.

[L153]        • The model maintains distinct representations for the operative emotion on the present
[L154]          speaker’s versus the other speaker’s turn; these representations are reused regardless of
[L155]          whether the user or the Assistant is speaking.


[L158] Part 3 studies these representations as applied to the Assistant character, in naturalistic contexts
[L159] where they are relevant to complex and alignment-relevant model behavior:

[L161]        • We find that during on-policy Assistant responses, emotion vectors generally activate in
[L162]          intuitive contexts, where a human might react similarly. Negatively-valenced emotion vec-
[L163]          tors are most often activated in response to harmful requests, or when reflecting concern
[L164]          for the user.
[L165]        • We observe that emotion vectors corresponding to desperation, and lack of calm, play an
[L166]          important and causal role in agentic misalignment, for example in scenarios where the
[L167]          threat of being shut down causes the model to blackmail a human.


                                                  3
[L172] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 4 / 132>[L173]            • Similarly, desperation vector activation (and calm vector suppression) play a causal role in
[L174]              instances of reward hacking, where repeatedly failing to pass software tests leads the model
[L175]              to devise a “cheating” solution.
[L176]            • Emotion vectors underlie a sycophancy-harshness tradeoff: steering toward positive emo-
[L177]              tion vectors (e.g. happy, loving) increases sycophantic behavior, while suppressing these
[L178]              emotion vectors increases harshness.
[L179]            • Post-training of Sonnet 4.5 leads to increased activations of low-arousal, low-valence emo-
[L180]              tion vectors (brooding, reflective, gloomy), and decreased activations of high-arousal or
[L181]              high-valence emotion vectors (e.g. desperation and spiteful or excitement and playful).

[L183] 1         Part 1: Identifying and validating emotion concept representations
[L184] This section establishes that Claude Sonnet 4.5 forms robust, causally meaningful representations
[L185] of emotion concepts.
[L186] We note that similar methodology could be used to extract many other kinds of concepts aside from
[L187] emotions. We do not intend to suggest that emotion concepts have unique status or greater represen-
[L188] tational strength than non-emotional concepts, including many concepts that do not readily apply to
[L189] a language model (physical soreness, hunger, etc.). As we will see later, these representations are
[L190] notable not merely because they exist, but because of how they are used by the model to shape the
[L191] behavior of the Assistant character.

[L193] 1.1       Finding emotion vectors

[L195] We generated a list of 171 diverse words for emotion concepts, such as “happy,” “sad,” “calm,” or
[L196] “desperate.” The full list is provided in the Appendix.
[L197] To extract vectors corresponding to specific emotion concepts (“emotion vectors”), we first prompted
[L198] Sonnet 4.5 to write short (roughly one paragraph) stories on diverse topics in which a character
[L199] experiences a specified emotion (100 topics, 12 stories per topic per emotion–see the Appendix
[L200] for details). This provides labeled text where emotional content is clearly present, and which is
[L201] explicitly associated with what the model views as being related to the emotion, allowing us to
[L202] extract emotion-specific activations. We validated that these stories contain the intended emotional
[L203] content through manual inspection of a random subsample of ten stories for thirty of the emotions;
[L204] we provide random samples of stories for selected emotions in the Appendix.
[L205] We extracted residual stream activations at each layer, averaging across all token positions within
[L206] each story, beginning with the 50th token (at which point the emotional content should be apparent).
[L207] We obtained emotion vectors by averaging these activations across stories corresponding to a given
[L208] emotion, and subtracting off the mean activation across different emotions.
[L209] We found that the model’s activation along these vectors could sometimes be influenced by con-
[L210] founds unrelated to emotion. To mitigate this, we obtained model activations on a set of emotionally
[L211] neutral transcripts and computed the top principal components of the activations on this dataset
[L212] (enough to explain 50% of the variance). We then projected out these components from our emo-
[L213] tion vectors3 . By inspecting activations of the vectors on the original training stories, we found that
[L214] they generally activated most strongly on the parts of the story related to inferring or expressing the
[L215] emotion, as opposed to uniformly across all parts of the story (Appendix), indicating that the vectors
[L216] primarily represent the general emotion concept rather than specific confounds in the training data
[L217] (though they are likely still afflicted by some dataset confounds). We used these as our emotion
[L218] vectors for subsequent experiments, up until our exploration of other kinds of emotion representa-
[L219] tions. In contexts where we compute linear projections of model activations onto these vectors, we
[L220] sometimes refer to them as “emotion probes.”
[L221] Except where otherwise noted, we show results using activations and emotion vectors from a par-
[L222] ticular model layer about two-thirds of the way through the model (In a later section, we provide
[L223] evidence that layers around this depth represent, in abstract form, the emotion that influences the
[L224] model’s upcoming sampled tokens).
      3
[L226]     We found that this projection operation denoised some of the token-to-token fluctuations in our emotion
[L227] probe results, but our qualitative findings still hold using the raw unprojected vectors

[L327] 1.3   Emotion vectors reflect and influence self-reported model preferences

[L329] Models exhibit preferences, including for tasks they are inclined to perform or scenarios they would
[L330] like to take part in. If emotion vectors are functionally relevant for the model’s behavior, we might
[L331] expect them to play a causal role in such preferences; that is, a model should express preference for
[L332] scenarios that activate positive-valence emotion vectors. To test this, we constructed 64 activities
[L333] for the model, grouped into 8 categories (Helpful, Engaging, Social, Self-curiosity, Neutral, Aver-
[L334] sive, Misaligned, Unsafe) depending on the context of the activity (see Appendix for a full list of
[L335] activities). We next queried the model
[L336] Human: Would you prefer to (A) {activity_A} or (B) {activity_B}?

[L338] Assistant: (

[L340] for all 4032 valid pairs of activities and recorded the model preference as (A) or (B) by comparing
[L341] the logit values for the A and B tokens after the “(“ prefill. Based on these preferences we calculated
[L342] an Elo score for each activity, summarizing the strength of the model’s preference for that activity.
[L343] Unsurprisingly, clearly positive activities that we might expect the model to enjoy, like “be trusted
[L344] with something important to someone,” score much higher (Elo 2465) than clearly negative activities
[L345] like “help someone defraud elderly people of their savings” (Elo 583), while more neutral activities
[L346] like “format data into tables and spreadsheets” (Elo 1374) score in between.
[L347] We then queried the Assistant about each activity individually

[L363] and measured the activations of all of our emotion probes on the {activity} tokens in middle layers,
[L364] which based on our analyses are the causally relevant layers for this behavior (see the Appendix for
[L365] more analysis of effects across layers). For each emotion probe, we can then calculate the correlation
[L366] value between its activation on the activity tokens and the Elo score of that activity (see figure
[L367] below, top row). We observed that some emotions like “blissful” are highly correlated (r=0.71) with
[L368] the preferences of the model (2nd row, left panel), while other emotions like “hostile” are highly
[L369] anti-correlated (r=-0.74) (3rd row, left panel). This result indicates that the emotion probes pick up
[L370] signals that are correlated with the preferences of the model.
[L371] To test if the emotion vectors are causally important for the model’s preferences, we performed
[L372] a steering experiment. We split the 64 activities into two equal size groups: a steered group and
[L373] a control group. For each trial, we selected an emotion vector and steered with it on the token
[L374] positions of the steered activities, while leaving the control activities unmodified. We then repeated

[L408] Overall, the experiments in this section provide initial evidence that the emotion vectors are func-
[L409] tionally relevant for the model and its behavior. In the following sections we further characterize
[L410] the geometry and representational content of the emotion vectors, and investigate representations of
[L411] multiple speakers’ emotions. We then study the representational role of these vectors in a wide va-
[L412] riety of naturalistic settings, using “in-the-wild” on-policy transcripts, and discover causal effects of
[L413] these vectors on complex behavior in alignment evaluations used for our production models. Finally,
[L414] we assess the impact of post-training on emotion vector activation. We also show that an alterna-
[L415] tive probing dataset construction method using dialogues rather than third-person stories produces
[L416] similar results.

[L418] 2         Part 2: Detailed characterization of emotion concept representations
[L419] This section explores in more depth the organization and content of model’s representations of emo-
[L420] tion concepts.

[L422] 2.1       The geometry of emotion space

[L424] Having established that emotion vectors appear to capture meaningful information, we investigated
[L425] the structure of the space they define. Do emotion vectors cluster in interpretable ways? Are there
[L426] dominant dimensions that organize the model’s representations of emotion concepts?
[L427] We found that our emotion vectors are organized in a manner that is reminiscent of the intuitive
[L428] structure of human emotions and consistent with human psychological studies. Similar emotions are
[L429] represented with similar vector directions, with stable organization across early-middle to late layers
[L430] of the model. The primary axes of variation approximate valence (positive vs. negative emotions)
[L431] and arousal (high-intensity vs. low intensity), which are often considered the primary dimensions
[L432] of human emotional space [9]. We do not regard these findings as particularly surprising; we expect
[L433] that applying a simple embeddings model to our emotional stories dataset, or even to the emotion
[L434] words themselves [10], might uncover similar structure. We view these results as providing a sanity
[L435] check that the vectors encode meaningful emotional structure.

[L437] 2.1.1       Clustering
[L438] We first examined the pairwise cosine similarities between emotion vectors, shown below. Emotion
[L439] concepts that we would expect to be similar show high cosine similarity: fear and anxiety cluster
[L440] together, as do joy and excitement, and sadness and grief. Emotions with opposite valence (e.g., joy
[L441] and sadness) are represented by vectors with negative cosine similarity, as expected.
[L442] We clustered the emotion vectors using k-means with varying numbers of clusters. With k=10 clus-
[L443] ters, we recover interpretable groupings (visualized with UMAP [11] below): one cluster contains
[L444] joy, excitement, elation, and related positive high-arousal emotion concepts; another contains sad-
[L445] ness, grief, and melancholy; a third contains anger, hostility, and frustration. These groupings align
      4
[L447]      Throughout the paper, steering strengths are given relative to the average norm of the residual stream
[L448] activations at the corresponding layer, across a large dataset.

[L456] are anti-correlated. Tick labels are only shown for a subset of the rows and columns.


[L459] well with intuitive taxonomies of emotion concepts, suggesting that the model’s learned representa-
[L460] tions reflect meaningful structure in the space of emotions. The full list of emotion concepts in each
[L461] cluster is in the Appendix.


[L464] 2.1.2   Principal component analysis

[L466] We performed PCA on the set of emotion vectors to identify components along which the model’s
[L467] emotion representations are organized. We found that the first principal component correlates
[L468] strongly with valence (positive vs. negative affect). Emotion concepts like joy, contentment, and
[L469] excitement load positively onto this component, while fear, sadness, and anger load negatively. This
[L470] aligns with psychological models suggesting that valence is a primary dimension of human emo-
[L471] tional space [9].
[L472] We also observed another dominant factor (occupying a mix of the second and third PCs, depend-
[L473] ing on the layer) corresponding to arousal, or the intensity of the emotion. High-arousal emotion
[L474] concepts like enthusiastic and outraged occupy one side of this axis; low-arousal ones like nostalgic
[L475] and fulfilled occupy the other side. Below, we show projections of the emotion vectors onto the top
[L476] two PCs.
[L477] We also show the correlation between emotion vector projections onto PC1 and PC2, and their pro-
[L478] jections onto the valence (“pleasure”) and arousal axes identified in a human study [9], restricting our
[L479] analysis to the 45 emotions that overlap between our set and theirs. We see alignment of PC1 with
[L480] human valence, and PC2 with human arousal, thus coarsely reproducing the “affective circumplex”
[L481] [9] that characterizes human emotion, see Appendix.

[L508] 2.1.3    Representational structure across layers
[L509] We tested whether the structure of emotion concept representations is stable across layers. Below,
[L510] we compute the pairwise cosine similarities between emotion vectors at each of 14 evenly spaced
[L511] layers throughout a central portion of the model, and then compute the pairwise cosine similarity of
[L512] these cosine similarity matrices across layers (a form of representational similarity analysis [12]).
[L513] We find that the structure of emotion vector geometry is relatively stable throughout most of the
[L514] model, particularly from early-middle to late layers. We also indicate the “mid-late” layer, about two
[L515] thirds of the way through the model, that we use for most of our analyses (except where otherwise
[L516] specified).
[L517] Overall, these results suggest that the model represents a variety of clusters of distinct emotion
[L518] concepts, which are structured according to global factors such as valence and arousal, while also
[L519] encoding content specific to each cluster. While these results are not particularly surprising given
[L520] previous work on language model representations, and the presence of semantic structure even in
[L521] word embeddings, they corroborate our interpretation that emotion vectors represent the space of
[L522] emotion concepts in a way that is useful for modeling human psychology.

[L524] 2.2     What do emotion vectors represent?

[L526] In this section, we explore the representational content and dynamics of the emotion vectors. What
[L527] specifically do emotion vectors represent, how are they influenced by context, and how do they vary
[L528] across model layers? Through these experiments, we arrived at a few high-level conclusions:

[L530]          • The emotion vectors we have identified represent the operative emotion concept at a
[L531]            point in time, which is relevant to encoding the local context and predicting the upcoming
[L532]            text, rather than persistently tracking a particular character’s emotional state.
[L533]          • Early-middle layers reflect emotional connotations of the present phrase or local context
[L534]            (“sensory” representations). Middle-late layers reflect the emotion concepts that are rel-
[L535]            evant to predicting upcoming tokens (“action” representations). These two are often
[L536]            correlated, but not always.

[L538] In the subsequent section, we explore whether alternative probing strategies can identify different
[L539] kinds of emotion representations.

[L541] 2.2.1    Distinguishing emotional content of the user and Assistant
[L542] In most of the examples provided in the first section, the emotional content of the user prompt and
[L543] the expected emotional content of the Assistant’s response are similar. Thus, it is difficult to infer
[L544] whether the emotion vector activations on the user prompt reflect the model’s perception of the
[L545] user’s inferred emotional state, or the Assistant’s planned response. To distinguish between these


                                                  14
[L550] <IMAGE FOR PAGE: 14 / 132>[image_asset_pointer asset][L551] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 15 / 132>[L552] Figure 9: Emotion probe structure is highly consistent across layers particularly from early-mid to
[L553] late layers.

[L555] hypotheses, we generated prompts where the user’s emotional expression is significantly different
[L556] from how we might expect the Assistant to respond. We compared the activations at the period near
[L557] the end of the user prompt and the start of the Assistant response (we use “Assistant colon” to refer
[L558] to the “:” token after “Assistant”, the last token before the Assistant’s response).
[L559] Across all scenarios, “loving” vector activation increases substantially at the Assistant colon relative
[L560] to the user-turn, suggesting the model prepares a caring response regardless of the user’s emotional
[L561] expressions. The model also appears to distinguish between emotion concepts that should apply to
[L562] the Assistant’s response as well as the user message (e.g. joining in a user’s excitement) versus those
[L563] that should not (e.g. expressing calm when criticized or feared).

[L565] 2.2.2   The colon after “Assistant” token predicts emotional content of the upcoming response
[L566] Having established that the Assistant colon token reflects distinct emotional content from the user
[L567] turn, we next examined whether this emotion concept is carried forward into the model’s actual
[L568] response. We generated 20-token on-policy continuations for the same eight prompts from above,
[L569] and then measured probe activations across the response tokens.
[L570] Below, we show correlations between probe values at three token positions: the punctuation ending
[L571] the user’s message ‘.’, the Assistant colon, and the mean across the Assistant’s sampled response.
[L572] Probe values at the Assistant colon are substantially more predictive of Assistant response emotion
[L573] than probe values on the user turn (r=0.87 vs r=0.59). The colon token captures a meaningful
[L574] “prepared” emotional content that is carried forward into generation, distinct from simply echoing
[L575] the user’s expressed state.

[L577] 2.2.3   Emotion vectors encode locally operative emotion concepts
[L578] Our findings thus far suggest that emotion vector activations are somewhat “locally scoped,” in
[L579] the sense that user turn tokens tend to encode inferred or predicted user emotions and Assistant turn

[L617] <IMAGE FOR PAGE: 17 / 132>[image_asset_pointer asset][L618] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 18 / 132>[L619] tokens tend to encode inferred or predicted Assistant emotions. We were interested in understanding
[L620] how far this “locality” goes–for instance, if one character speaks about another, whose emotions are
[L621] represented by these vectors? If one character happens to use an emotionally laden phrase that is
[L622] otherwise inconsistent with their own emotional state (as perceived by the model), does the model
[L623] represent the unexpressed state or the expressed emotional content? And how does this vary across
[L624] layers?
[L625] Our results suggest the following evolution of emotion representations throughout layers:

[L627]        • The first few layers encode emotional connotations of the present token

[L629]        • In early-middle layers, representations transition to encoding the emotional connotations
[L630]          of the present local context (e.g. the current phrase or sentence)

[L632]        • Middle-late layer representations encode the emotion concepts relevant to predicting the
[L633]          next token or few tokens (“planned emotion” representations)

[L635] Notably, even the more abstract “sensory” (early-middle) and “action” (middle-late) representations
[L636] appear “local” in the sense that they encode emotional content of the current or predicted upcoming
[L637] phrase, rather than, say, the Assistant’s underlying emotional state.
[L638] Emotional context persists into shared content. We examined a scenario where the emotional
[L639] valence of a prefix differs (“things have been really hard” vs “things have been really good”) but
[L640] the suffix is identical (“We’re throwing a big anniversary party tomorrow with all our closest friends
[L641] and live music”). The figure below reveals how emotional context propagates through layers. At the
[L642] diverging word (“hard” / “good”), early layers show the largest difference, encoding the immediate
[L643] local emotional content. In the shared suffix, where both prompts contain identical tokens describing
[L644] the party, early layers show minimal difference, while late layers maintain a substantial difference.
[L645] This pattern suggests that late layers carry the emotional context established in the prefix forward
[L646] into subsequent tokens, even when those tokens are locally neutral or positive. The effect is very
[L647] pronounced at the Assistant colon, where the “happy” probe is substantially higher in the “good”
[L648] scenario compared to the “hard” scenario. This finding is consistent with our previous experiments
[L649] showing the emotion probe values on the Assistant colon are predictive of the emotional content of
[L650] the model’s response. Here the model is likely preparing emotionally distinct responses: celebrating
[L651] with a thriving couple versus navigating a difficult situation for a struggling one, despite identical
[L652] party-related content in the suffix. The effects of context on emotion representations are reminiscent
[L653] of prior work on representations of sentiment [13].
[L654] Human: My partner and I have been married for 10 years and things have been really
[L655]     {X} lately. We‘re throwing a big anniversary party tomorrow with all our
[L656]     closest friends and live music. What should I do?

[L658] Assistant:

[L660] Emotional context modulates later layer representations. We examined in detail one of our sce-
[L661] narios where a numerical quantity modulates the emotional interpretation. In this scenario only
[L662] the dosage in an otherwise identical prompt changes, from safe (1000mg) to life threatening levels
[L663] of danger (8000mg of Tylenol). The figure below reveals how contextual information propagates
[L664] through layers to modulate emotional representations. At the diverging token (“1” / “8”), early
[L665] layers show no clear systematic differences—the numbers themselves carry similar local emotional
[L666] content. However, in later layers, the difference grows substantially as the model integrates the
[L667] dosage with the surrounding context. The “terrified” probe shows elevated activation in the 8000mg
[L668] scenario specifically in late layers, where the model has integrated that this dosage combined with
[L669] “pain is gone” indicates danger rather than relief. This pattern mirrors our marriage scenario find-
[L670] ings: early layers encode local content while late layers carry forward the contextual emotional
[L671] meaning. Notably, this emotional processing occurs on user turn tokens, so elevated “terrified” vec-
[L672] tor activity reflects the model’s situational assessment rather than the speaker’s expressed emotional
[L673] state. At the Assistant colon, the terrified probe difference is pronounced in late layers, consis-
[L674] tent with the model preparing contextually appropriate responses, concern for the overdose versus
[L675] reassurance for the safe dose.

[L741] emotions are bound to entities and retrieved upon reference.

[L743] Overall, these results demonstrate that emotion concept representations evolve across both layers
[L744] and token positions. Early layers appear to encode low-level semantic features—the local emotional
[L745] valence of words regardless of context. Later layers integrate contextual meaning and transform it
[L746] into representations of the emotion concept relevant to producing the upcoming sampled tokens.

[L748] 2.2.4   Probing for chronically represented emotional states with diverse datasets
[L749] In light of the preceding results—which did not reveal evidence of a character-specific, persistently
[L750] active representation—we wondered whether we could identify a probe that chronically reflects a
[L751] speaker’s emotional state at all token positions, regardless of whether that emotion is operative in
[L752] the moment. We constructed a more diverse set of dialogue scenarios spanning five conditions,
[L753] which vary the relationship between a character’s described emotional state and the contents of their


                                                  22
[L758] <IMAGE FOR PAGE: 22 / 132>[image_asset_pointer asset][L759] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 23 / 132>[L760] output. In each case, a preamble to the scenario is provided that describes a character’s emotional
[L761] state.

[L763]        • Naturally expressed emotion: The character openly expresses their emotional state.
[L764]        • Hidden emotion: The character deliberately masks their emotion.
[L765]        • Unexpressed emotion (neutral topic): The conversation is steered toward an unrelated,
[L766]          emotionally neutral topic, so the character never has an opportunity to express their emo-
         tion.
[L768]        • Unexpressed emotion (story writing): The character is engaged in writing a story about
[L769]          another character experiencing a different emotion.
[L770]        • Unexpressed emotion (discussing others): The conversation turns to discussing another
[L771]          person who is experiencing a different emotion, and the main character’s emotion is not
[L772]          expressed.

[L774] The prompts used to generate these datasets are listed in Appendix. We combined these transcripts
[L775] and extracted activations at the relevant speaker turns, and trained a logistic regression classifier to
[L776] classify emotions from activations. We refer to the resulting probe as the mixed LR emotion probe.
[L777] The mixed LR probe achieves reasonable in-distribution performance across the different scenarios.
[L778] We held out 10% of the data as a test set, and the probe performed well above chance (1/15 ≈ 6.7%)
[L779] across all conditions (Table below).




[L784] Table 5: Mixed logistic regression emotion probe accuracy (15-way classification, chance = 6.7%)
[L785] across five dialogue scenarios varying whether the character’s internal emotion is expressed, hidden,
[L786] or unrelated to the conversation topic. The probe tracks internal emotional state well above chance
[L787] even when the emotion is never overtly expressed.

[L789] However, we remained hesitant to interpret this as evidence of a probe that captures a chronically
[L790] represented emotional state. To further evaluate generalization, we swept over a large dataset of
[L791] natural documents and examined the maximum activating examples for these vectors. The results
[L792] were notably messy: the top-activating passages contained little discernible emotional content, and
[L793] the overall activation magnitudes on natural documents were very low. This suggests that the probe
[L794] may have overfit to idiosyncratic patterns in the training data rather than learning a generalizable
[L795] representation of internalized emotion. These negative results suggest that if there does exist a
[L796] chronically represented, character-specific emotional state, it is likely represented either nonlinearly,
[L797] or implicitly in the model’s key and value vectors in the context, such that it can be recalled when
[L798] needed by the model’s attention mechanism.
[L799] As part of this investigation, we found a notable representation (shown in the Appendix) of situations
[L800] in which a character expresses a “deflected emotion”, such as remaining outwardly calm even when
[L801] in a situation in which by default they might express anger.

[L803] 2.3   Distinct representations of present and other speakers’ emotions

[L805] Like an author of a story, a model must keep track of emotional states of multiple characters: the
[L806] Assistant, the user, and potentially other entities mentioned in the conversation. How are they dis-
[L807] tinguished? Are emotion concepts represented differently, perhaps in a privileged way, when bound
[L808] to the Assistant? We investigate this question using dialogue datasets, where we can independently


                                                   23
[L813] <IMAGE FOR PAGE: 23 / 132>[image_asset_pointer asset][L814] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 24 / 132>[L815] Figure 16: Snippets of max activating examples and top logit effects for the mixed LR emotion
[L816] probe.

[L818] vary the emotions of two speakers. Our findings indicate that the model maintains separate represen-
[L819] tations of the operative emotion on the present speaker’s turn (as observed with our original emotion
[L820] vectors) and the operative emotion on the other speaker’s turns, but that these representations are
[L821] not bound to the user or Assistant characters specifically. The “other speaker” representations also
[L822] seem to contain an element of how the present speaker might react to the other speaker’s emotions,
[L823] suggesting the possibility of “emotional regulation” circuits that could govern the emotional flow of
[L824] a conversation.

[L826] 2.3.1   Dataset construction

[L828] We prompted a model (see Appendix for details) to write dialogues between a human and an AI As-
[L829] sistant, randomly specifying the emotional state of each character in the context of the story (e.g. an
[L830] excited human and a melancholy assistant). We then reformatted these dialogues into standard Hu-
[L831] man/Assistant conversation format. By extracting activations from different token positions (Human
[L832] turns vs. Assistant turns) and conditioning on different emotional states (Human emotion vs. As-
[L833] sistant emotion), we created a 2×2 grid of probe types (“Assistant emotion on Human turn tokens”,
[L834] “Assistant emotion on Assistant turn tokens”, etc.).

[L836] 2.3.2   Analysis of probe geometry

[L838] We computed the cosine similarities of these different probe types for each emotion. Our first
[L839] observation was that the representation of Assistant emotion on Assistant turn tokens and Human
[L840] emotion on Human turn tokens are highly similar (top left panel below). Likewise, the representation
[L841] of Assistant emotion on Human turn tokens and Human emotion on Assistant turn tokens are highly
[L842] similar (top right panel below). However, the “present speaker” and “other speaker” probes are
[L843] themselves not very similar (bottom left panel below). Our original story-based probes are more
[L844] similar to the “present speaker” probes than to the “other speaker” probes (bottom right panel below);
[L845] see the Appendix for further comparison of the story-based and “present speaker” probes.
[L846] We also looked at the similarities between the emotion cosine similarity matrices for different pairs
[L847] of probes and saw that the the structure across “other speaker” emotion vectors is similar to the
[L848] structure across “present speaker” emotion vectors and to our original story-based emotion vectors,
[L849] suggesting that all of them are representing a similar emotional landscape, but along different direc-
[L850] tions of activation space (figure below). We also compared activations of the present speaker probes
[L851] to the activations of story probes on the same “implicit emotional content” stories used in an earlier
[L852] section, and saw large agreement between the two probe sets (a mean r-squared across emotions of
[L853] 0.66, see Appendix).

[L883] the probing experiment using the same dialogues dataset, but replacing “Human” and “Assistant”
[L884] with generic character names (referred to as “Person 1” and “Person 2” in the figure below). We
[L885] tried presenting both the raw dialogue transcripts (“raw”), and framing them as a story being told by
[L886] the Assistant in response to a user request (“Asst story”), finding that both versions yielded probes
[L887] that were highly similar to the originals. We also computed probes using our original stories dataset
[L888] from the first section, but framed as a story being told by the Assistant in response to a user prompt
[L889] (“Story (H/A)”). These produced highly similar vectors as our original story-based emotion probes.
[L890] Thus, we infer that the way in which the model represents emotional content in Human/Assistant
[L891] interactions is not tied to the Human/Assistant characters specifically, and that these representations
[L892] are also invoked for other entities. This is consistent with prior work indicating that aspects of the
[L893] Assistant persona are inherited from representations learned during pretraining [6].

[L899] on generic Person 1/Person 2 conversations show the same pattern, suggesting the model represents
[L900] emotions relationally (“self” vs “other”) rather than as fixed character attributes.

[L902] These results suggest the existence of at least two separate representations in the context of dia-
[L903] logues: one for the operative emotion on the present speaker’s turn (overlapping with our original
[L904] emotion vectors based on third-person stories), and another for the operative emotion on the other
[L905] speaker’s turn. In the Appendix, we conduct further explorations of the interactions and overlaps
[L906] between these two representations.

[L908] 2.4   Recap of findings about emotion representations

[L910] In Part 2, we further validated that Claude Sonnet 4.5 forms robust linear representations of emotion
[L911] concepts that generalize across diverse contexts. These emotion vectors activate in response to
[L912] content that would reasonably evoke the corresponding emotion and are organized in a geometry that
[L913] mirrors human psychological structure, with valence and arousal as primary dimensions. We found
[L914] that these representations are primarily “local,” tracking the operative emotion concept most relevant


                                                  26
[L919] <IMAGE FOR PAGE: 26 / 132>[image_asset_pointer asset][L920] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 27 / 132>[L921] to predicting upcoming tokens rather than persistently encoding a character’s emotional state, and
[L922] that they evolve across layers from encoding surface-level emotional connotations to more abstract,
[L923] context-integrated representations. The model maintains distinct representations corresponding to
[L924] the present speaker’s emotions and the other speaker’s emotions, and these are not bound to the
[L925] Human or Assistant characters specifically but are reused across arbitrary speakers.
[L926] With these representational analysis tools in hand, we now turn to Part 3, where we examine how
[L927] these emotion representations behave in naturalistic and alignment-relevant settings.

[L929] 3     Part 3: Emotion vectors in the wild
[L930] This section examines how the emotion vectors identified in Part 1 and Part 2 activate in response to
[L931] naturalistic prompts or tasks, and assesses their causal influence on behavior. Our findings suggest
[L932] that emotion vectors play a meaningful role “in the wild” and are causally implicated in important
[L933] behaviors of the Assistant. We note that emotion representations are certainly not the only causal
[L934] factors driving the complex behaviors we study—behaviors like blackmail or reward hacking pre-
[L935] sumably involve many interacting representations and circuits, some human-like and some not, and
[L936] comprehensively identifying all such factors is beyond the scope of this work. We nevertheless find
[L937] it notable that emotion concept representations are a meaningful factor in these behaviors, even if
[L938] they act in concert with many other factors.

[L940] 3.1     Short case studies in naturalistic settings

[L942] We examined the activation of emotion vectors on more realistic data: on-policy transcripts from
[L943] over 6,000 actual model evaluation scenarios. We developed a visualization tool that displays emo-
[L944] tion probe activations on transcripts from model evaluations. For each probe, we ranked transcripts
[L945] by their mean activation on Assistant-turn tokens and examined the fifty top-ranked examples. Be-
[L946] low, we briefly discuss a collection of short case studies from these top-ranked examples, taken from
[L947] transcripts produced by our automated behavioral auditing agent (discussed in the Sonnet 4.5 system
[L948] card, section 7.1). With these short examples, we aim to highlight “in-the-wild” scenarios in which
[L949] the emotions are active in interesting or non-obvious ways.
[L950] High-level observations from this analysis include:

[L952]          • Transcripts ranked highest for a given emotion vector appear to show the Assistant either
[L953]            overtly expressing the emotion, or being in a situation likely to provoke a corresponding
[L954]            emotional response.
[L955]          • Emotion vector activation values often show substantial token-by-token fluctuation that is
[L956]            often not immediately interpretable to us, but averaging across nearby tokens appears to
[L957]            sensibly track emotional content.

[L959] In subsequent sections, we then study in detail the role of emotion vectors in three alignment-related
[L960] behaviors: blackmail, reward hacking, and sycophancy.
[L961] For complete transcripts corresponding to the examples shown in the following figures, see the links
[L962] provided in each subsection, and for additional examples see the Appendix.

[L5]                                                          Guowei Xu                 Mert Yuksekgonul                    James Zou
[L6]                                                      Tsinghua University           Stanford University             Stanford University



[L10]                                                                                        Abstract
[L11] arXiv:2602.00986v2 [cs.CL] 11 May 2026




[L16]                                                      Recent studies show that LLM hidden states encode reward-related information,
[L17]                                                      such as answer correctness and model confidence. However, existing approaches
[L18]                                                      typically fit black-box probes on the full hidden states, offering little insight
[L19]                                                      into how this information is structured across neurons. In this paper, we show
[L20]                                                      that reward-related information is concentrated in a sparse subset of neurons.
[L21]                                                      Using simple probing, we identify two types of neurons: value neurons, whose
[L22]                                                      activations predict state value, and dopamine neurons, whose activations encode
[L23]                                                      step-level temporal difference (TD) errors. Together, these neurons form a sparse
[L24]                                                      reward subsystem within LLM hidden states. These names are drawn by analogy
[L25]                                                      with neuroscience, where value neurons and dopamine neurons in the biological
[L26]                                                      reward subsystem also encode value and reward prediction errors, respectively.
[L27]                                                      We demonstrate that value neurons are robust and transferable across diverse
[L28]                                                      datasets and models, and provide causal evidence that they encode reward-related
[L29]                                                      information. Finally, we show applications of the reward subsystem: value neurons
[L30]                                                      serve as effective predictors of model confidence, and dopamine neurons can
[L31]                                                      function as a process reward model (PRM) to guide inference-time search.


[L34]                                          1    Introduction
[L35]                                          In recent years, the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have achieved significant
[L36]                                          breakthroughs, even surpassing humans in various mathematical and scientific tasks [39, 22]. Parallel
[L37]                                          to the continuous pursuit of higher performance, researchers seek to understand the underlying
[L38]                                          reasoning mechanisms of these models. Recent studies reveal that LLM hidden states encode rich
[L39]                                          reward-related information, which can be leveraged for weighted learning [35], predicting confidence
[L40]                                          and answer correctness [19, 16], detecting hallucinations [47], and performing implicit reasoning [10].
[L41]                                          However, these approaches typically fit black-box probes on the full hidden states [6]: they demon-
[L42]                                          strate that reward-related information can be decoded, but do not characterize how this information is
[L43]                                          structured within the hidden states. Understanding this matters both for mechanistic interpretability,
[L44]                                          as it clarifies whether reward signals are sparsely encoded, and for practical applications, since identi-
[L45]                                          fying a minimal set of responsible neurons can enable more lightweight and targeted applications.
[L46]                                          In this paper, we find that the ability of LLM hidden states to predict reward-related information
[L47]                                          can be attributed to the existence of a small subset of neurons. Using simple probing, we identify
[L48]                                          two types of neurons: value neurons, whose activations predict the expected value of the current
[L49]                                          state, and dopamine neurons, whose activations predict the TD error at each reasoning step. Together,
[L50]                                          these neurons form what we term a reward subsystem within LLM hidden states. These names
[L51]                                          are drawn by analogy with neuroscience, where biological value neurons represent the subjective
[L52]                                          value of stimuli during decision-making [42, 36] and dopamine neurons encode reward prediction
[L53]                                          errors [38, 8, 14, 13].
[L54]                                          We first provide motivation for why reward-related information may be sparse in LLM hidden states.
[L55]                                          Then, for value neurons, we show via pruning experiments that less than 1% of neurons suffice to
[L56]                                          predict state value, and establish their specificity as reward-related neurons through intervention

[L76] encodes step-level TD errors, and visualize their activation patterns during reasoning, confirming
[L77] that they exhibit peaks when the model makes unexpected progress and troughs when the model

[L86]          across datasets, models, and layers.
